full_judgment:
In this application the pe-emptor has challenged the propriety of the order dated 15-1-1970 passed by Mr. J. C. Bhowmick, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Appeal No.125 of 1969 reversing the order dated 31-5-1969 passed by Mr. S.D.M.N. Islam, Munsiff, 1st Court, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No.236 of 1963 allowing pre emotion under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 

 4. The learned Munsiff, Chandpur accepted the case of the preemptor and by his order dated 31-5-1969 allowed the pre-emption as prayed for. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge, Comilla reversed the order of the learned Munsiff by his order dated 31-5-1969 passed in Misc. Appeal No. 125 of 1969. The decision of the learned Subordinate Judge is mainly resisted on the ground that the alleged separation of the holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not valid and as such was not binding upon the co-sharers, and in the absence of valid separation of the holding, the pre-emptees continued to be co-sharer in the holding and their purchase from opposite-party No.5, a co-sharer in the holding, is not liable to be pre-empted. The pre-emptor being aggrieved by that decision moved this court when this Rule was issued. 

 5. Mr. Aminul Huque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner finds it rather difficult to support the contention of the petitioner that the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge to the effect that in the absence of all the co-sharers the 4 separation cases were not legal and valid, and consequently the holding recorded in C.S. Khatian No.26 continued to be in existence, is bad in law. From the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that the question about validity of the separation cases was specifically raised and the same has been answered It has been noticed in the judgment that the 4 sons of Abbas Ali did not make the other daughters and widows of Abbas Ali party to the separation cases filed under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It was not disputed that Zahura Khatoon and Ramjan Banu, the two widows and Halima, Omarenessa and Gadi, the 3 daughters were not made parties in the said 4 separation case. Section of the penal Tenancy Act makes it imperative that to make a valid division of at mire of holding or a distribution of the feat payable in respect thereof there must be express consent in writing of all the co-sharers. Sub section (2) of section 88 provides that the Court, on an application made to it by one or more co-sharer tenants for a division of a tenure or holding it for a distribution of the rent payable in respect thereof, or for the annulment or modification of a previous division or distribution other than one made under this sub-section or under an agreement made between all the landlords and co-sharer tenants in conformance with the provisions of sub- section (1), may by an order in writing, direct such division of the tenure or holding or such distribution of rent as she court considers fair and equitable, provided  that no such order shall be passed without notice to the landlord or the entire body of landlords or their common agent, if any, and to the remaining co-sharer tenants; and that nothing contained in the sub-section shall be deemed to authorise a court on application for division or distribution to direct a division or distribution in respect of the share of any tenant other than an application under this sub-section or a co-sharer tenant who has been joined as a co-applicant under sub-section (2). Sub-section (3) provides that on receipt of notice of an application for division of distribution under sub-section (2) a co-sharer tenant may apply to be joined as a co-applicant, and upon such application the court shall join the said co-sharer tenant as a co-applicant without further notice to the landlord or landlord sand he remaining co-sharer tenants. Thus it appears that the above provisions do not authorise the Civil Court to allow division of holding without giving notice to all the co-sharer tenants and clause (c) of the proviso to sub-section (2) puts a limitation upon the authority of the Civil Court that nothing contained in the sub-section shall be deemed to authorise a court to direct a division or distribution in respect of the share of any tenant other than an application under this subsection or a co-sharer tenant who has been joined as a co-applicant under sub-section (3). 

 6. The pre-emptor could not adduce any evidence to show that the notice was issued upon the co-Sharers who had been left out in the application filed under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and that they applied as provided under sub-section (3) of Section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Therefore, in the absence of those co-share tenants the orders of separation passed by the Civil  Court under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act were not valid under the law, and as such the same are not binding upon all the co-sharer tenants Besides as pointed out above section 88(2), proviso (c) prohibits the court from making an order for distribution of rent in respect of the share of co-share tenants who has not joined by filing an application in the proceedings, as provided in sub-section (3), This question as considered by Henderson, J. of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Sri Rajeswar Tankur and another Vs. Lakshmi Kanta Pramanik and others, A.I.R. 1944 Cal, 287. It was argued before the Court that the proviso (c) merely means that the question will not be res judicata so far as a tenant within the terms of the provision is concerned, but the learned Judge did not accept this argument and held as follows:- 

 In that view of the matter the learned District Judge has rightly held that the order passed in the four separation cases under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act were not valid in law and consequently the holding appertaining to C.S.Khatian No.26 continued as before. And as such opposite parties 1-4 were not strangers to the holding as alleged by the pre-emptor, and the disputed sale is not liable to be pre-empted. 

 8. In the face of the language of section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as pointed out above mere presumption for non-production of dakhilas showing payment of rent of the undivided holding will not be sufficient to deprive the pre-emptess from pleading that the alleged order of separation of the holding was not valid, and as such the same was not binding upon the co-shares. I do not find any substance in the contention also. So far the question of estoppel is concerned, I do not find any substance in this point also, simple answer is that there is no estoppel against statute. Mr. Aziz, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee opposite parties referred me to a decision of the Bombay High Court, in the case of Lady Dibai Dinshaw Peti & others Vs. The Dominion of India and another reported in A.I.R 1951 Bombay 72. It appears from this decision that a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court consisting of Chagla, C.J. and bhagwati J. has held that “no person be precluded from pleading that certain orders are illegal or invalid, because the question as to whether orders are illegal or invalid or invalid is a pure question of law and there can be no estoppel against law.”
